pennsylvania.title: Pennsylvania Personal Injury Claims: Full Tort, Limited Tort and Deadlines
pennsylvania.metaTitle: Pennsylvania Personal Injury Laws 2026: Tort Options Guide
pennsylvania.metaDescription: How Pennsylvania’s full and limited tort options, 51% fault bar, Fair Share Act, two-year deadline, 15/30/5 insurance and government caps affect a claim.
pennsylvania.excerpt: In Pennsylvania, the tort option on your policy can decide whether you recover pain and suffering at all. The state also bars recovery above 50% fault, gives you two years to sue and has no cap on damages. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
pennsylvania.html:
How a Pennsylvania injury claim is valued

A Pennsylvania injury claim covers economic loss (medical bills, lost earnings and earning capacity, property damage) and non-economic loss (pain, suffering, embarrassment, disfigurement and loss of life’s pleasures). Pennsylvania’s constitution forbids the Legislature from capping damages for injury or death outside workers’ compensation, so there is no limit on pain and suffering, including in medical malpractice cases.

For car crashes, one choice made when the policy was bought often matters more than anything that happened in the crash: whether the injured person chose “full tort” or “limited tort”. Limited tort is cheaper but gives up most pain and suffering claims unless the injury is serious. Add the 51% fault bar, the Fair Share Act and a two-year deadline, and Pennsylvania rewards people who check their paperwork early. This guide covers each rule with the statute behind it.

Run your own figures with the Pennsylvania car accident calculator, which asks about your tort option, or the Pennsylvania personal injury calculator.

A Pennsylvania crash claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver is rear-ended at a light in Philadelphia and treats for neck and back strain for four months. Medical bills are $14,000 and lost wages $4,000. The driver’s own first-party medical benefits paid the first $5,000. The other driver’s insurer says the injured driver stopped short and argues for 20% fault.

  • Total economic loss: $18,000. First-party benefits already paid can’t be claimed from the other driver, leaving $13,000.
  • With full tort: pain and suffering at two to three times the economic loss adds $36,000 to $54,000. After 20% fault: $39,200 to $53,600.
  • With limited tort and no serious injury: only the unpaid economic loss is recoverable. After 20% fault: about $10,400.

Same crash, same injury, and the difference is several times over. If the injury did qualify as serious, for example because it caused a lasting impairment, the limited tort driver would be back to the full tort range. If a jury found the driver 51% at fault, either way the recovery from the other driver would be zero.

Full tort and limited tort

Pennsylvania is a choice no-fault state. When you buy a policy you pick a tort option for yourself and your household (75 Pa.C.S. § 1705):

  • Full tort keeps the right to sue an at-fault driver for every kind of damage, including pain and suffering for any injury.
  • Limited tort lowers the premium. You can still recover all economic losses from the at-fault driver, but you can recover non-economic damages only if you suffered a “serious injury”: death, serious impairment of a body function, or permanent serious disfigurement (§ 1702).

Whether an injury is a serious impairment is usually a question for the jury, considering how much the injury affected your daily life and for how long (Washington v. Baxter, 1998). There are exceptions where limited tort doesn’t apply, including when the at-fault driver is convicted of driving under the influence or accepts Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition (ARD) for it, when the at-fault vehicle is registered in another state, when the at-fault driver had no insurance, and when you were injured as an occupant of a commercial vehicle rather than a private car. Check the declarations page of every policy in the household; a family member’s full tort choice doesn’t always carry over.

How the choice is made, and what if no one chose

Insurers must give you a written notice explaining the two options when the policy is issued, and the election is made on a signed form. If the named insured never makes a valid election, the policy is treated as full tort. You can change the option going forward at any time, usually at renewal, but the option in force on the day of the crash is the one that counts; a switch after the crash doesn’t help. The election made by the named insured generally applies to relatives living in the household who don’t have their own policy.

Proving a serious injury under limited tort

Because the threshold turns on how the injury affected your life, the strongest evidence is ordinary and specific: missed work, activities you had to stop, help you needed at home, how long symptoms lasted and what the treating doctors expect going forward. Surgery, a fracture, nerve damage confirmed by testing and lasting restrictions all help. Short gaps in treatment and a quick return to normal activities are what insurers point to when they argue the injury wasn’t serious.

First-party benefits: your own policy pays first

Every Pennsylvania auto policy includes at least $5,000 of first-party medical benefits, which pay your medical bills regardless of fault (§ 1711). Many people buy more, along with optional income loss, accidental death and funeral benefits. Providers are paid at a fee schedule tied to Medicare rates.

Two rules follow from that. First, you can’t recover from the at-fault driver the amounts your first-party benefits paid or were obligated to pay (§ 1722). Second, the insurer that paid those benefits generally can’t take reimbursement from your injury settlement (§ 1720), and in auto cases that protection extends to many health plans as well. Self-funded employer plans governed by federal law, Medicare and Medical Assistance can still claim reimbursement. The no-fault and PIP calculator shows how first-party benefits fit into a claim.

Fault: the 51% bar and the Fair Share Act

Under 42 Pa.C.S. § 7102, you can recover if your negligence is not greater than the combined negligence of the defendants. At 50% you recover half; at 51% you recover nothing. Your damages are reduced by your share of fault.

The 2011 Fair Share Act changed how defendants share the bill. Each defendant pays only its own percentage, unless it is 60% or more at fault, in which case it is liable for the whole award (§ 7102(a.1)). A few exceptions keep joint liability, such as intentional torts and certain dram shop claims. In a crash where a driver is 55% at fault and a road contractor 45%, each pays only its own share, so the injured person bears the risk that one of them can’t pay. The comparative fault calculator shows how a split changes the result.

Pennsylvania doesn’t let the defense use the fact that you weren’t wearing a seat belt as evidence of negligence or to reduce damages (75 Pa.C.S. § 4581(e)).

Pennsylvania filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: two years from the injury (42 Pa.C.S. § 5524).
  • Wrongful death and survival claims: two years, generally from the date of death (§ 5524).
  • Property damage: two years (§ 5524).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from when the injury was or should have been discovered, with a seven-year outer limit in most cases (MCARE Act, 40 P.S. § 1303.513). A certificate of merit from a qualified professional must be filed within 60 days of the complaint (Pa.R.C.P. 1042.3).
  • Claims against the Commonwealth or a local agency: written notice within six months of the injury, stating the claim, to the agency and, for the Commonwealth, the Attorney General (42 Pa.C.S. § 5522). Courts can excuse a late notice for reasonable cause in some cases, but don’t rely on it.

The Pennsylvania filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

Car insurance minimums and UM/UIM

Pennsylvania requires liability coverage of at least $15,000 per person, $30,000 per crash and $5,000 for property damage (§ 1702), among the lowest minimums in the country. A driver who carries only the minimum can pay no more than $15,000 to one injured person, which is why uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage matters so much here.

Insurers must offer UM and UIM equal to your liability limits, and you have it unless you signed the specific statutory rejection forms (§ 1731). Stacking, which combines the UM/UIM limits for each vehicle on the policy, also applies unless you waived it in writing (§ 1738). A rejection or waiver form that doesn’t match the statutory wording can be void, so these forms are worth reviewing after any serious crash. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the available coverage can pay.

Medical bills: what the jury hears

Pennsylvania limits past medical damages to the amount actually paid and accepted as full payment when a provider has agreed to take a reduced rate. In Moorhead v. Crozer Chester Medical Center (2001), the Pennsylvania Supreme Court held that a patient whose Medicare-reduced bills had been paid in full could not recover the higher billed amount. The same logic is applied to other negotiated payments. In car crash cases, the first-party benefits fee schedule, which ties provider payments to Medicare rates (§ 1797), also keeps the amounts lower than the sticker price.

The collateral source rule still protects you in other ways. The jury doesn’t hear that health insurance paid your bills, and the at-fault party doesn’t get credit for insurance you paid for. Future medical costs are proven with a doctor’s testimony and often a life care plan, and they aren’t limited by past discounts.

Trucks, buses and other commercial vehicles

Commercial vehicle crashes are where Pennsylvania claims most often exceed the personal policy minimums. Interstate trucking companies must carry at least $750,000 in liability coverage under federal rules, and the company can be liable for its own negligence in hiring, training, maintenance and hours-of-service compliance. If you were riding in a commercial vehicle, such as a bus, rather than a private passenger car, limited tort generally doesn’t restrict your claim. Rideshare companies also carry policies with far higher limits once a ride has been accepted. Ask for the policy information in writing and send a preservation letter for logs and electronic data early. The Pennsylvania truck accident calculator uses the federal limits.

Claims against government in Pennsylvania

The Commonwealth and local agencies are immune from most injury claims, with listed exceptions. For the Commonwealth, the exceptions include vehicle accidents, medical care by Commonwealth employees, dangerous conditions of Commonwealth real estate, highways and sidewalks, and potholes the Commonwealth had notice of (§ 8522). Local agencies have similar exceptions for vehicles, real property, streets, sidewalks, traffic controls and utility facilities (§ 8542).

Recovery is capped: $250,000 per person and $1,000,000 per incident against the Commonwealth (§ 8528), and $500,000 in total per incident against a local agency (§ 8553). Against a local agency, pain and suffering is recoverable only in cases of death or permanent loss of a bodily function, permanent disfigurement or permanent dismemberment, and only when medical expenses exceed $1,500 (§ 8553). That makes it essential to identify any private defendant, such as a contractor, as well.

Medical malpractice in Pennsylvania

There is no cap on compensatory damages in Pennsylvania malpractice cases; the state constitution bars one. Punitive damages against an individual health care provider are capped at 200% of the compensatory damages (40 P.S. § 1303.505). Future medical costs above $100,000 can be paid over time as they are incurred rather than in a lump sum.

Since January 1, 2023, malpractice cases can be filed in any county where venue would be proper under the general rules, after the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ended the special rule that limited them to the county where the care took place. The malpractice calculator reflects that there is no damages cap.

Wrongful death and survival claims

When someone dies because of another’s negligence, Pennsylvania allows two claims, usually filed together by the personal representative:

  • A wrongful death claim (42 Pa.C.S. § 8301) for the spouse, children and parents, covering medical, funeral and estate administration costs and the value of the services, support, society and comfort the person would have given the family.
  • A survival claim (§ 8302) for the estate, covering the person’s pain and suffering before death and their lost earning capacity over their expected working life, minus personal maintenance costs.

The survival claim is often the larger of the two for a younger person with years of earnings ahead. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, snow and ice, dog bites and bars

Falls. A business owes customers reasonable care, including inspecting for and fixing dangers it knew or should have known about. For snow and ice, Pennsylvania’s “hills and ridges” doctrine generally protects an owner from liability for a fall on a natural accumulation during generally slippery conditions, unless the snow or ice was allowed to build into ridges or elevations that weren’t cleared within a reasonable time. See the Pennsylvania slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. The Dog Law makes owners liable for the medical costs of a bite without proof of fault. Other damages, such as pain and suffering, need proof that the owner was negligent or knew the dog was dangerous. See the Pennsylvania dog bite calculator.

Bars. A licensed seller can be liable for serving alcohol to a visibly intoxicated person who then injures someone (47 P.S. § 4-493(1) and § 4-497).

Arbitration, delay damages and timing

Smaller cases often go to compulsory arbitration first. Counties can require arbitration before a panel of lawyers for claims up to $50,000 (42 Pa.C.S. § 7361), and either side can appeal for a new trial. Larger cases go to a jury.

In bodily injury cases that reach a verdict, the court adds delay damages under Rule 238, calculated at the prime rate plus one percent, from one year after the defendant was served. A defendant can stop delay damages from running by making a written offer that the plaintiff then fails to beat by more than 25%. Settlements for minors need court approval (Pa.R.C.P. 2039). The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage.

Liens and what you keep

  • Auto first-party benefits: no reimbursement from your settlement (§ 1720).
  • Workers’ compensation: if you were hurt on the job, the comp carrier has a lien on a third-party recovery, including from a car crash, reduced by its share of the attorney fees and costs.
  • Medical Assistance (Medicaid) and Medicare: both can claim reimbursement, and both reduce their claims for the cost of getting the recovery.
  • The lawyer’s fee and costs, usually one third to 40% on a contingency basis.

The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves. Before accepting an offer, check it against your estimate with the settlement offer checker.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Find the declarations page for every auto policy in your household and check the tort option and the UM/UIM and stacking elections.
  • Submit medical bills to your own auto insurer for first-party benefits.
  • If a government vehicle, road or property was involved, send the six-month written notice.
  • Track how the injury affects work, sleep, chores and activities. Under limited tort, that record is the evidence of a serious impairment.
  • Calendar the two-year deadline from the crash date.
  • Ask the other driver’s insurer in writing for the policy limits, and your own insurer for your UIM limits and whether stacking applies.
  • If you were hurt at work, report the injury to your employer and the comp carrier as well; the comp lien will shape the settlement.

faqs.question: What is the difference between full tort and limited tort in Pennsylvania?
faqs.answer: Full tort keeps your right to sue for pain and suffering for any injury. Limited tort saves premium but allows pain and suffering only for a serious injury: death, serious impairment of a body function or permanent serious disfigurement. Both allow recovery of economic losses (75 Pa.C.S. § 1705).

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Pennsylvania?
faqs.answer: Two years from the injury in most cases, including wrongful death and survival claims (42 Pa.C.S. § 5524). Claims against the Commonwealth or a local agency need written notice within six months.

faqs.question: Can I recover if I was partly at fault in Pennsylvania?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your share is 50% or less; your damages are reduced by your percentage. At 51% or more you recover nothing from that defendant (42 Pa.C.S. § 7102).

faqs.question: Does Pennsylvania cap pain and suffering?
faqs.answer: No. Pennsylvania’s constitution bars caps on damages for injury or death, including in malpractice cases. Claims against government agencies are limited to $250,000 per person against the Commonwealth and $500,000 per incident against local agencies.

faqs.question: Does my car insurer get repaid from my settlement?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Section 1720 bars reimbursement of first-party auto benefits from a tort recovery, and you can’t claim those amounts from the other driver either. Medicare, Medical Assistance and some federally governed employer plans can still claim reimbursement.

faqs.question: Can the insurer argue I wasn’t wearing a seat belt?
faqs.answer: Not to reduce your damages. Pennsylvania law makes the failure to wear a seat belt inadmissible as evidence of negligence in a civil case (75 Pa.C.S. § 4581(e)).

illinois.title: Illinois Personal Injury Claims: Fault, Deadlines and No Damage Caps
illinois.metaTitle: Illinois Personal Injury Laws 2026: Fault, Caps and Deadlines
illinois.metaDescription: How Illinois’s 51% fault bar, two-year deadline, one-year government limit, 25/50/20 insurance, 6% prejudgment interest and 40% lien cap affect a claim.
illinois.excerpt: Illinois has no caps on injury damages and adds 6% prejudgment interest once a lawsuit is filed, but it bars recovery above 50% fault and gives only one year to sue local governments and bars. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
illinois.html:
How an Illinois injury claim is valued

An Illinois injury claim recovers economic damages (medical expenses, lost earnings and the cost of future care) and non-economic damages, which Illinois juries consider in separate categories: pain and suffering, emotional distress, disfigurement, and loss of a normal life. There is no cap on any of them. The Illinois Supreme Court has struck down every attempt to cap injury damages, first in Best v. Taylor Machine Works (1997) and then, for medical malpractice, in Lebron v. Gottlieb Memorial Hospital (2010).

What shapes Illinois settlements most is a mix of rules that cut both ways. The 51% fault bar can end a claim. A defendant less than 25% at fault may pay only its share. But since 2021, defendants who don’t make a reasonable offer early face 6% prejudgment interest, and since 2023 families in most wrongful death cases can seek punitive damages. This guide explains each rule and the statute behind it.

Run your own figures with the Illinois personal injury calculator or the Illinois car accident calculator, which open with Illinois rules applied.

An Illinois claim, worked through

An example, not a forecast. A cyclist is hit by a turning car in Chicago and fractures a collarbone, which needs surgery. Medical expenses total $42,000 and the cyclist loses $15,000 in wages. The driver’s insurer says the cyclist ran a yellow light and argues for 35% fault.

  • Economic damages: $42,000 plus $15,000 = $57,000.
  • Non-economic damages at two to three times the economic losses: $114,000 to $171,000.
  • Claim before fault: $171,000 to $228,000.
  • After a 35% reduction: $111,150 to $148,200.

If the jury found the cyclist more than 50% responsible, the recovery would be zero. If the case went to trial instead of settling, prejudgment interest would also come into play. Say the defendant offered $250,000 in writing within a year of filing, the cyclist turned it down, and the jury later returned a $400,000 judgment: interest at 6% a year from the filing date would run only on the $150,000 by which the judgment beat the offer. Illinois also requires most drivers to carry only $25,000 per person in bodily injury coverage, so the cyclist’s own underinsured motorist coverage, if the household has a car policy, may decide how much of this claim is collectible.

Fault: the 51% bar

Illinois uses modified comparative fault. If your own fault is more than 50% of the cause of the injury, you can’t recover. At 50% or less, your damages are reduced by your percentage (735 ILCS 5/2-1116). The rule covers negligence claims and product liability claims based on strict liability.

Unlike many states, Illinois doesn’t let the defense use the fact that you weren’t wearing a seat belt as evidence of negligence or to reduce your damages (625 ILCS 5/12-603.1). Fault arguments come instead from traffic signals, speed, lookout and right of way, which is why intersection video and event data from vehicles matter so much in Illinois crash claims. The comparative fault calculator shows how a fault finding changes the result.

When one defendant pays for others

Under 735 ILCS 5/2-1117, a defendant whose fault is less than 25% of the total fault attributable to the plaintiff, the defendants and certain third parties is liable only for its share of non-medical damages. It remains jointly liable for all past and future medical expenses. A defendant at 25% or more is jointly and severally liable for everything. Medical malpractice defendants are jointly liable regardless of percentage (§ 2-1118). In practice, Illinois plaintiffs try to keep a well-insured defendant above the 25% line.

Illinois filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: two years from the injury (735 ILCS 5/13-202).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (740 ILCS 180/2), with longer periods in some cases involving violent intentional acts.
  • Property damage: five years (735 ILCS 5/13-205).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from when you knew or should have known of the injury, but no more than four years after the care. For children, the outer limit is eight years, and no later than the child’s 22nd birthday (735 ILCS 5/13-212).
  • Cities, counties, park districts and other local public entities: one year to file suit (745 ILCS 10/8-101).
  • Chicago Transit Authority: written notice within six months and a lawsuit within one year (70 ILCS 3605/41).
  • The State of Illinois: claims go to the Court of Claims. A personal injury claimant must file written notice with the Attorney General and the court clerk within one year (705 ILCS 505/22-1) and file the claim within two years.
  • Dram shop claims against a bar: one year from the injury (235 ILCS 5/6-21).

The one-year limits catch people out. A crash involving a city truck or a bus, a fall on a park district path and a claim against a bar all have half the time of an ordinary claim. The Illinois filing deadline calculator counts the dates.

Car insurance in Illinois

Illinois is an at-fault state. Drivers must carry at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $20,000 for property damage (625 ILCS 5/7-601 and 7-203). Every policy must also include uninsured motorist coverage at least equal to the minimum bodily injury limits (215 ILCS 5/143a).

Underinsured motorist coverage in Illinois works as gap coverage: it pays up to your UIM limit minus what the at-fault driver’s insurer paid (215 ILCS 5/143a-2). With $100,000 of UIM and a $25,000 policy on the other side, UIM can add up to $75,000. If your UIM limit is the same as the other driver’s liability limit, it adds nothing. That is a reason to carry UIM well above the state minimum. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows how the coverages fit together.

Your UM and UIM coverage usually protects you and relatives in your household even when you aren’t in your own car, for example as a pedestrian, a cyclist or a passenger in someone else’s vehicle, subject to the policy’s terms. Medical payments coverage, which pays medical bills regardless of fault, is optional in Illinois; if you have it, it is often the fastest money available after a crash. A hit-and-run is handled as an uninsured motorist claim, which usually requires reporting the crash to police promptly and notifying your insurer within the time the policy sets. Read the notice section of your policy early, because a late report can give the insurer a reason to deny.

Medical bills: Illinois allows the reasonable value

Illinois is more favorable than many states on medical expenses. In Wills v. Foster (2008), the Illinois Supreme Court held that an injured person can recover the reasonable value of medical services, and that the full billed amount is evidence of that value, even if Medicare, Medicaid or a health insurer paid the provider less. The collateral source rule keeps the jury from hearing about the discount, and the defendant doesn’t get credit for it. The defense can still challenge whether the charges were reasonable and the care necessary, and the billed amounts have to be supported by testimony or records showing they were paid or are owed.

That rule doesn’t mean you keep the difference. Providers, health plans and government programs may hold liens or reimbursement rights against the recovery, covered below.

Hurt at work: comp and third-party claims

An employee hurt on the job usually can’t sue the employer, because workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy. But a claim against someone else who caused the injury, such as another driver, a property owner or an equipment maker, is allowed alongside the comp claim. When that third-party case recovers money, the employer or its comp insurer is repaid what it paid in benefits, minus 25% for attorney fees and a share of the costs (820 ILCS 305/5(b)). Illinois also limits how much a negligent employer can be made to contribute to the third party’s judgment to the amount of its comp liability (Kotecki v. Cyclops Welding, 1991). The construction accident calculator takes the comp lien into account.

No caps on damages

Illinois has no cap on compensatory damages in any injury case, including medical malpractice, because the Illinois Supreme Court has repeatedly held that legislative caps violate the separation of powers in the state constitution. Juries decide the value of pain, suffering and loss of a normal life, and judges review only for awards that are excessive.

Punitive damages are available for willful and wanton or intentional conduct, but a plaintiff must ask the court for permission to add a punitive damages claim and show a reasonable likelihood of proving it at trial (735 ILCS 5/2-604.1). They aren’t allowed in medical or legal malpractice cases (§ 2-1115). Claims against the State of Illinois in the Court of Claims are subject to a statutory limit on awards, which is one more reason to identify every private defendant.

Prejudgment interest since 2021

Since July 1, 2021, Illinois adds prejudgment interest of 6% a year to personal injury and wrongful death judgments (735 ILCS 5/2-1303(c)). It runs from the date the lawsuit was filed, for up to five years, on compensatory damages. Punitive damages, sanctions and statutory fees and costs are excluded, and local public entities don’t pay it.

Defendants can limit it with a written settlement offer made within 12 months of filing. If the plaintiff doesn’t accept the offer within 90 days and later wins more, interest runs only on the amount above the offer. If the judgment is equal to or less than the offer, there is no prejudgment interest at all. The rule gives insurers a strong reason to make a real offer early in an Illinois lawsuit, and plaintiffs a reason to take a close look at that offer. The settlement offer checker compares an offer against your estimate.

Wrongful death and survival claims

The Illinois Wrongful Death Act lets the personal representative recover for the surviving spouse and next of kin. Damages include lost financial support and services and, since 2007, grief, sorrow and mental suffering (740 ILCS 180/2). The court divides the recovery among the family according to their dependency on the person who died.

Since August 11, 2023, Public Act 103-0514 also allows punitive damages in wrongful death actions and lets punitive damages claims survive in the estate’s survival action. The change doesn’t apply to medical or legal malpractice claims or to claims against the state or local governments and their employees. The survival action (755 ILCS 5/27-6) recovers the person’s own medical costs, lost earnings and pain and suffering between the injury and death. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Medical malpractice in Illinois

Besides the two-year discovery rule and four-year outer limit, Illinois requires a malpractice complaint to be filed with an attorney’s affidavit and a written report from a qualified health professional stating that there is a reasonable and meritorious cause for the claim (735 ILCS 5/2-622). There is no cap on damages, and defendants in malpractice cases are jointly and severally liable. Punitive damages aren’t available. The malpractice calculator reflects that Illinois has no cap.

Falls, snow, dog bites and bars

Falls on property. Under the Premises Liability Act, owners owe people lawfully on their property reasonable care under the circumstances (740 ILCS 130/2). For snow and ice, owners generally aren’t liable for natural accumulations, only for unnatural accumulations they created or made worse, such as runoff from a downspout that freezes. The Snow and Ice Removal Act also protects residential owners who shovel the public sidewalk in front of their home unless their removal was willful or wanton (745 ILCS 75). See the Illinois slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. The Animal Control Act makes owners strictly liable when a dog, without provocation, attacks or injures someone peaceably conducting themselves where they have a right to be (510 ILCS 5/16). It doesn’t matter whether the dog had bitten before. See the Illinois dog bite calculator.

Bars. The Dram Shop Act makes sellers liable without proof of negligence when the alcohol they sold caused the intoxication that led to an injury (235 ILCS 5/6-21). The trade-off is that recovery is capped at amounts adjusted each year by the state Comptroller, far below the value of a serious injury, and the claim must be filed within one year.

Medical liens and what you keep

Illinois limits how much of a settlement medical providers can take. Under the Health Care Services Lien Act, all liens of hospitals, doctors and other providers together can’t exceed 40% of the verdict or settlement, and no single type of provider can take more than one third. When liens hit the 40% limit, physicians and other professionals share 20% and hospitals and other providers share 20% (770 ILCS 23/10). The limits don’t cover Medicare, Medicaid, workers’ compensation or private health insurer reimbursement claims, which have their own rules.

A typical settlement also pays the lawyer’s contingency fee, commonly one third, and case costs. The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves you. Settlements for children require court approval.

Arbitration and how long claims take

Many Illinois crash claims settle with the insurer within months after treatment ends. Smaller lawsuits are often sent to court-annexed mandatory arbitration before a panel of attorneys, under Supreme Court Rules 86 to 95, with each judicial circuit setting its own maximum claim amount. Either side can reject the award and go to trial, though the rejecting party may pay a fee. Larger cases in Cook County and the collar counties can take two to four years to reach trial. The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage.

Trucks, CTA buses and rideshare

Commercial vehicles bring larger policies and more defendants. Interstate trucking companies must carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage under federal rules, and the company can be liable for its own failures in hiring, training, maintenance and hours-of-service compliance. A CTA bus crash is a claim against a public body with a six-month notice and one-year filing deadline. Rideshare companies carry far higher limits once a ride has been accepted than while a driver is only logged in. The Illinois truck accident calculator uses the federal limits.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Check whether a public body is involved: a city vehicle, a CTA bus, a park district or a public road. If so, the deadline is one year, and six months’ notice for the CTA.
  • Find your own auto policy and check the UIM limit. In Illinois it only helps if it is higher than the other driver’s liability limit.
  • If alcohol was involved, identify where the driver was served. The dram shop claim has a one-year deadline.
  • Photograph the scene, including any snow, ice or downspout runoff after a fall.
  • Keep every medical bill and lien notice. The 40% lien limit only helps if you know what each provider claims.
  • Keep itemized bills, not just balances. Under Wills v. Foster the billed amount is evidence of reasonable value, but only with the paperwork behind it.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Illinois?
faqs.answer: Two years from the injury in most cases (735 ILCS 5/13-202). Claims against cities and other local public entities have one year, the CTA requires notice within six months, and dram shop claims against bars must be filed within one year.

faqs.question: Can I recover if I was partly at fault in Illinois?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your fault is 50% or less; your damages are reduced by your percentage. If you are more than 50% at fault you recover nothing (735 ILCS 5/2-1116).

faqs.question: Does Illinois cap pain and suffering damages?
faqs.answer: No. The Illinois Supreme Court struck down damage caps in Best v. Taylor Machine Works (1997) and, for medical malpractice, in Lebron v. Gottlieb Memorial Hospital (2010).

faqs.question: Does Illinois award interest on injury verdicts?
faqs.answer: Yes. Since July 1, 2021, judgments earn 6% a year in prejudgment interest from the filing date for up to five years. A written defense offer made within 12 months of filing limits interest to the amount the judgment exceeds the offer.

faqs.question: How much of my settlement can medical providers take in Illinois?
faqs.answer: Under the Health Care Services Lien Act, all provider liens together can’t exceed 40% of the recovery, and no single type of provider can take more than one third. Medicare, Medicaid, workers’ comp and health insurers follow their own rules.

faqs.question: Can a family get punitive damages in an Illinois wrongful death case?
faqs.answer: Yes, since August 11, 2023, in most cases. Public Act 103-0514 excludes medical and legal malpractice claims and claims against the state and local governments.

ohio.title: Ohio Personal Injury Claims: Damage Caps, Fault and Deadlines
ohio.metaTitle: Ohio Personal Injury Laws 2026: Damage Caps and Deadlines
ohio.metaDescription: How Ohio’s $250,000–$350,000 non-economic cap, catastrophic injury exception, 51% fault bar, two-year deadline and 25/50/25 insurance shape a claim.
ohio.excerpt: Ohio caps pain and suffering in most injury cases at $250,000 to $350,000 unless the injury is catastrophic, bars recovery above 50% fault and gives you two years to sue. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
ohio.html:
How an Ohio injury claim is valued

An Ohio injury claim recovers economic loss (medical care, lost wages, lost earning capacity and other expenses) and non-economic loss (pain and suffering, loss of society and companionship, mental anguish, and inconvenience). The total is reduced by your share of fault, and above 50% fault the claim ends.

The rule that sets Ohio apart is its cap on non-economic damages. In most injury cases, pain and suffering is limited to the greater of $250,000 or three times your economic loss, with a ceiling of $350,000 per person, unless the injury is catastrophic. That cap doesn’t apply to wrongful death, and Ohio has separate rules for medical malpractice, government defendants and punitive damages. This guide explains each with the statute behind it.

Run your own figures with the Ohio personal injury calculator or the Ohio car accident calculator. Both apply the Ohio cap automatically.

An Ohio claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver is hit head-on on a two-lane road outside Columbus and needs a two-level spinal fusion. Medical expenses come to $78,000 and lost wages to $22,000, so economic loss is $100,000. The defense argues the injured driver drifted toward the center line and was 20% at fault.

  • A jury might value the pain, limitation and lost enjoyment of life at three to five times the economic loss: $300,000 to $500,000.
  • Ohio’s cap is the greater of $250,000 or three times economic loss ($300,000), no more than $350,000. Here that is $300,000.
  • Capped claim before fault: $100,000 economic plus $300,000 non-economic = $400,000.
  • After a 20% reduction: about $320,000.

Without the cap, the same facts would produce $320,000 to $480,000 after fault. The cap disappears entirely if the injury is catastrophic, meaning a permanent and substantial physical deformity, loss of use of a limb, loss of a bodily organ system, or a permanent injury that prevents the person from caring for themselves. Whether a fusion with lasting restrictions crosses that line is one of the most argued questions in Ohio injury cases, and the answer can change the value by hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The cap on non-economic damages

Ohio Revised Code § 2315.18 limits compensatory damages for non-economic loss in tort actions to the greater of $250,000 or three times the plaintiff’s economic loss, up to $350,000 per plaintiff and $500,000 per occurrence. There is no cap for:

  • Permanent and substantial physical deformity, loss of use of a limb, or loss of a bodily organ system
  • A permanent physical functional injury that permanently prevents the injured person from independently caring for themselves and performing life-sustaining activities

The section also doesn’t apply to wrongful death actions, to claims against the state in the Court of Claims, or to claims against political subdivisions, which have their own rules. The Ohio Supreme Court upheld the cap in Arbino v. Johnson & Johnson (2007) and again in Brandt v. Pompa (2022). The jury isn’t told about the cap; the court applies it after the verdict. Economic damages are never capped. Bills to raise the caps and index them to inflation, such as SB 292 and HB 447, were pending in 2026 but hadn’t become law as of August 2026.

How the cap plays out in negotiation

Insurers value most Ohio injury claims with the cap in mind. For an injury with modest economic losses, the cap is $250,000 of non-economic damages no matter how a jury might feel, so the insurer’s top number is usually the economic loss plus something under that figure, reduced for fault. As economic losses grow, the cap rises with them until it reaches $350,000 at about $116,700 of economic loss. A spouse’s claim for loss of consortium is a separate plaintiff’s claim with its own limit, but all claims from one occurrence share the $500,000 ceiling. When the facts support the catastrophic exception, the negotiation changes completely, which is why medical evidence of permanence is the center of so many Ohio cases.

Fault: the 51% bar

Ohio bars recovery when the plaintiff’s fault is greater than the combined fault of everyone else whose conduct caused the harm. At 50% or less, damages are reduced by the plaintiff’s percentage (R.C. § 2315.33). The jury can assign fault to people who aren’t parties if the defense proves it.

When several defendants are at fault

Under R.C. § 2307.22, a defendant more than 50% at fault is jointly and severally liable for all economic damages, and a defendant 50% or less at fault pays only its own share of economic damages. For non-economic damages, every defendant pays only its own share, whatever its percentage. If an uninsured driver is 60% at fault and a negligent road contractor 40%, the contractor pays 40% of everything, and the uninsured driver’s share may be uncollectable without your own UM coverage.

Seat belts

In Ohio, not wearing a seat belt can’t be used as evidence of negligence, but the jury can consider it on causation and reduce the non-economic damages that a belt would have prevented. Economic damages aren’t reduced (R.C. § 4513.263(F)). The comparative fault calculator shows how a fault finding changes the result.

Ohio filing deadlines

  • Personal injury and property damage: two years (R.C. § 2305.10).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (R.C. § 2125.02).
  • Assault and battery: one year (R.C. § 2305.111).
  • Medical malpractice: one year from when the patient discovered or should have discovered the injury, or the end of the doctor-patient relationship, whichever is later. Sending the provider a written notice, called a 180-day letter, before the year runs out extends the deadline by 180 days from the notice. There is a four-year outer limit in most cases (R.C. § 2305.113).
  • Cities, counties, townships and other political subdivisions: two years (R.C. § 2744.04).
  • The State of Ohio: two years in the Court of Claims (R.C. § 2743.16).

The one-year malpractice deadline is among the shortest in the country. The Ohio filing deadline calculator counts the dates from your injury.

Car insurance in Ohio

Ohio is an at-fault state. Drivers must be able to show financial responsibility of at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage (R.C. § 4509.51). Many drivers carry only that, so a serious injury claim often runs into the at-fault driver’s limit.

Ohio insurers aren’t required to offer uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage at all, a change made in 2001. Many policies include it, but you need to check. When you have UIM, its limit is generally reduced by what the at-fault driver’s insurer pays, so a $100,000 UIM limit against a $25,000 liability payment adds up to $75,000 (R.C. § 3937.18). The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows what the available coverage can pay.

Truck crashes bring federal minimums of at least $750,000 for interstate freight carriers, and the trucking company’s own hiring, training and hours-of-service compliance become part of the claim. The Ohio truck accident calculator uses those limits.

Rideshare crashes work in tiers. The company’s coverage is modest while a driver is only logged into the app and waiting, and much higher from the moment a ride is accepted until the passenger gets out, so the trip records from the app often decide how much coverage is available. The rideshare accident calculator walks through the tiers.

Medical bills: billed and paid amounts

Ohio lets the jury hear both what was billed and what was accepted as payment. In Robinson v. Bates (2006), the Ohio Supreme Court held that both the original bill and the amount accepted as full payment are admissible to prove the reasonable value of medical care, and the jury decides the figure. Jaques v. Manton (2010) confirmed that written-off amounts can be shown to the jury. In practice the medical figure in an Ohio verdict often lands between the two.

Ohio also allows a defendant to introduce evidence of some collateral benefits, such as insurance payments, unless the source has a right to be repaid from the recovery (R.C. § 2315.20). The interaction between these rules is technical, and it affects claims with large written-off balances most.

Medical malpractice in Ohio

Malpractice claims have their own non-economic damages cap under R.C. § 2323.43: the greater of $250,000 or three times economic loss, up to $350,000 per plaintiff and $500,000 per occurrence. For catastrophic injuries, the limits rise to $500,000 per plaintiff and $1,000,000 per occurrence. Economic damages aren’t capped. The complaint must be accompanied by an affidavit of merit from a qualified expert (Civil Rule 10(D)(2)). The malpractice calculator applies the Ohio formula.

Claims against government in Ohio

Ohio’s political subdivisions, such as cities, counties, townships and school districts, are immune from most injury claims under R.C. chapter 2744, with exceptions (§ 2744.02(B)) that include:

  • Negligent driving by an employee on the job, with protection for police, fire and emergency responders unless their conduct was willful or wanton
  • Negligent performance of proprietary functions, such as operating a utility
  • Negligent failure to keep public roads in repair and remove obstructions
  • Injuries caused by physical defects in government buildings used for governmental functions

When an exception applies, non-economic damages are limited to $250,000 per person except in wrongful death actions, there is no catastrophic-injury exception to that limit, punitive damages aren’t allowed, and the award is reduced by collateral benefits such as health insurance (§ 2744.05). Claims against the State of Ohio itself go to the Court of Claims, where a judge rather than a jury decides the case. These limits make it important to identify any private party, such as a contractor, who shares fault.

Punitive damages

Punitive damages require proof by clear and convincing evidence of malice, aggravated or egregious fraud, or similar conduct, and the jury must first award compensatory damages. They are capped at twice the compensatory damages. Against an individual or a small employer, the cap is the lesser of twice compensatory damages or 10% of net worth, up to $350,000 (R.C. § 2315.21). Drunk driving with a high blood alcohol level and deliberate safety violations are where they most often arise.

Wrongful death and survival claims

A wrongful death action in Ohio is brought by the personal representative for the surviving spouse, children and parents, who are presumed to have suffered damages, and for other next of kin (R.C. § 2125.02). Damages include lost support and services, loss of society (companionship, care, guidance, counsel and the like), loss of prospective inheritance, the family’s mental anguish, and funeral costs. The § 2315.18 cap doesn’t apply, which makes wrongful death one of the few Ohio injury claims with no limit on non-economic damages. A separate survival claim (R.C. § 2305.21) recovers the person’s own pain, suffering and expenses before death. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. An Ohio property owner generally has no duty to warn of dangers that are open and obvious, because the danger itself is the warning (Armstrong v. Best Buy Co., 2003). Owners also generally owe no duty to remove natural accumulations of snow and ice. Claims usually turn on hidden hazards, unnatural accumulations and conditions the owner created. See the Ohio slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. Owners, keepers and harborers are strictly liable for injuries their dog causes, whether or not the dog was known to be dangerous, unless the injured person was trespassing, committing a crime on the property, or teasing or abusing the dog there (R.C. § 955.28). A negligence claim is also possible. See the Ohio dog bite calculator.

Bars. Ohio’s dram shop law is narrow. A liquor permit holder is liable for injuries off its premises only if it knowingly sold alcohol to a noticeably intoxicated person or to someone underage, and that sale caused the injury (R.C. § 4399.18).

Hurt at work in Ohio

Ohio is one of a handful of states where workers’ compensation runs through a state fund, the Bureau of Workers’ Compensation, rather than private insurers, though large employers can self-insure. An employee generally can’t sue the employer for a workplace injury; the exception is an employer intentional tort, which requires proof that the employer acted with deliberate intent to injure (R.C. § 2745.01). A claim against a third party who caused the injury, such as a negligent driver, a property owner or an equipment maker, is allowed alongside the comp claim. The BWC or the self-insured employer then has a statutory right to be repaid from that recovery, and the statute sets a formula for dividing a recovery that falls short of full value (R.C. § 4123.931). The construction accident calculator takes the comp lien into account.

Liens, subrogation and what you keep

Ohio has a statute that protects injured people whose recovery falls short. When a settlement is less than the full value of the claim, because of comparative fault, limited insurance or other reasons, an insurer or health plan’s subrogation claim is reduced in the same proportion (R.C. § 2323.44). If your claim was worth $400,000 but settled for $100,000 because of policy limits, a health plan’s $40,000 claim can be reduced to $10,000. Self-funded employer plans governed by federal law and Medicare may not be bound by this rule.

Settlements for children need probate court approval (R.C. § 2111.18). The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves you.

Interest, timing and settlement offers

Ohio awards prejudgment interest in tort cases only when the court finds that the party required to pay failed to make a good faith effort to settle, and the other side didn’t (R.C. § 1343.03(C)). That gives a reasonable, documented demand real weight: an insurer that refuses to engage can end up paying interest from the date the claim arose. Use the settlement offer checker to compare an offer with your estimate and the settlement timeline calculator to estimate how long each stage takes.

A 2026 law, HB 105, adds rules for third-party litigation funding agreements, where an outside company advances money against a future settlement, starting October 6, 2026. If you are considering such an advance, read its terms closely.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Check your auto policy for UM and UIM coverage. Ohio doesn’t require insurers to include it.
  • For a malpractice concern, talk to a lawyer quickly. The deadline is one year, and a 180-day letter must go out before it expires.
  • Ask your doctors to document permanent limitations clearly. The catastrophic-injury exception to the cap depends on that record.
  • Keep both the bills and the explanations of benefits. Ohio juries can see both numbers.
  • If a government vehicle or road was involved, identify the agency and any private contractor early.
  • If you were hurt at work, file the comp claim with the BWC or your self-insured employer, and keep the third-party claim on a separate track.
  • Write down how the injury limits daily life, week by week. Juries in capped cases still decide the non-economic number, and the record supports it.

georgia.title: Georgia Personal Injury Claims After SB 68: Fault, Deadlines and Damages
georgia.metaTitle: Georgia Personal Injury Laws 2026: SB 68, Fault and Deadlines
georgia.metaDescription: How Georgia’s 50% fault bar, two-year deadline, 2025 SB 68 changes, add-on UM coverage, ante litem notices and full-value-of-life rule affect a claim.
georgia.excerpt: Georgia bars recovery at 50% fault, gives you two years to sue and needs notice to a city within six months. Its 2025 tort reform, SB 68, also changed seat belt evidence and medical damages. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
georgia.html:
How a Georgia injury claim is valued

Georgia injury claims recover special damages, Georgia’s term for provable money losses such as medical expenses and lost wages, and general damages for pain and suffering, which Georgia leaves to the “enlightened conscience” of the jury. There is no cap on general damages in ordinary injury cases. The total is reduced by your share of fault, and at 50% fault the claim ends.

Georgia changed a great deal in 2025. Senate Bill 68, signed on April 21, 2025, let juries hear seat belt evidence, limited medical damages to the reasonable value of necessary care with evidence of what was actually paid, restricted how lawyers can suggest dollar amounts for pain and suffering, and created rules for negligent security cases. Some parts apply to every pending case and some only to claims that arose after the law took effect. This guide covers those changes and the older Georgia rules that still shape settlements, with the statute behind each.

Run your own figures with the Georgia personal injury calculator or the Georgia car accident calculator.

A Georgia crash claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver is sideswiped on I-285 and treats for a shoulder injury that later needs arthroscopic surgery. The providers billed $36,000; the driver’s health plan paid $15,000. Lost wages are $8,000. The crash happened in 2026, so the post-2025 medical damages rule applies. The other driver’s insurer says the injured driver was speeding and not wearing a seat belt, and argues for 30% fault.

  • Medical damages are now the reasonable value of necessary care, and the jury can consider the $15,000 actually paid alongside the $36,000 billed.
  • Economic damages fall somewhere between $23,000 (paid basis) and $44,000 (billed basis).
  • With pain and suffering at about two times the economic damages, the claim before fault ranges from $69,000 to $132,000.
  • After a 30% reduction: $48,300 to $92,400.

Before SB 68, the seat belt argument couldn’t have been raised at all and the medical figure would usually have been the billed amount. Now both can lower the value. And if the jury puts the driver at 50% or more, there is no recovery. The minimum liability policy in Georgia is $25,000 per person, so on a claim this size the injured driver’s own uninsured motorist coverage may matter as much as the at-fault driver’s policy.

Fault: the 50% bar and apportionment

Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, a plaintiff who is 50% or more responsible for the injury recovers nothing. Below 50%, damages are reduced by the plaintiff’s percentage. Georgia’s bar is stricter than the 51% rule used in many states: a jury finding of exactly 50% ends the claim.

Georgia also apportions fault among every responsible person, including nonparties such as an unidentified driver or someone who already settled, if the defense gives notice and proves their share. Each defendant pays only its own percentage; Georgia generally doesn’t make one defendant pay another’s share. If a phantom driver who cut you off is assigned 40% and the driver who hit you 60%, the driver who hit you pays 60%, and your own uninsured motorist coverage is the usual source for the rest.

Seat belts after SB 68

For decades Georgia barred evidence that an injured person wasn’t wearing a seat belt. SB 68 amended O.C.G.A. § 40-8-76.1 so that seat belt use or non-use is now admissible on negligence, comparative negligence, causation, assumption of risk and apportionment of fault, subject to the usual rules of evidence. Insurers still can’t cancel a policy or raise rates because someone wasn’t belted. The comparative fault calculator shows how a fault finding changes the value.

Georgia filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: two years from the injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (§ 9-3-33).
  • Property damage, such as a car: four years (§ 9-3-31).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from the injury or death, with a five-year outer limit (§ 9-3-71). The complaint must include an expert’s affidavit setting out at least one negligent act (§ 9-11-9.1).
  • Claims against a city: written ante litem notice within six months (§ 36-33-5).
  • Claims against a county: written notice within 12 months (§ 36-11-1).
  • Claims against the State of Georgia: written ante litem notice within 12 months to the Department of Administrative Services and the agency involved (§ 50-21-26).

Georgia also pauses the deadline while a criminal prosecution arising from the same incident is pending, for up to six years, when the injured person is the victim of the crime (§ 9-3-99). It can apply after a crash where the other driver was charged, but courts have read it narrowly at times, so don’t rely on it without advice. The Georgia filing deadline calculator counts the standard dates.

Car insurance and uninsured motorist coverage

Georgia is an at-fault state. Drivers must carry at least $25,000 per person, $50,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage (O.C.G.A. § 33-34-4). That minimum is often far below the value of an injury that needs surgery.

Georgia’s uninsured motorist law (§ 33-7-11) is unusually helpful once you understand it. Policies include UM coverage at the same limits as your liability coverage unless you reject it in writing. Since 2009 the default is add-on coverage, which pays on top of the at-fault driver’s liability limits. The alternative, reduced-by coverage, subtracts the other driver’s limits and must be chosen in writing. With $100,000 of add-on UM and a $25,000 policy on the other side, up to $125,000 is available; with reduced-by coverage, only $100,000. Check which type you have, and whether household policies stack. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator handles both types.

Truck and rideshare crashes

Commercial vehicles carry far more insurance than the $25,000 personal minimum. Interstate freight carriers must carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage under federal rules, and the trucking company can be liable for its own negligence in hiring, training, maintenance and hours-of-service compliance. Georgia also allows an injured person to name a motor carrier’s insurer directly as a defendant in many cases (O.C.G.A. §§ 40-1-112 and 40-2-140), which is unusual; in most states the insurer stays out of the lawsuit. Rideshare companies carry modest coverage while a driver is only logged into the app and much higher limits once a ride is accepted. Send a preservation letter for driver logs, electronic data and dashcam video quickly. The Georgia truck accident calculator uses the federal limits, and the rideshare accident calculator walks through the coverage tiers.

Medical damages after SB 68

For claims arising on or after April 21, 2025, a new statute, O.C.G.A. § 51-12-1.1, limits special damages for medical care to the reasonable value of medically necessary care, as decided by the jury. The jury may consider the amounts actually paid or needed to satisfy the charges, such as the rate a health insurer paid, not just the billed amount. When care was provided under a letter of protection, where the provider waits to be paid from the settlement, the letter, the itemized charges and any sale of the bill to a third party can be discovered and, in some cases, shown to the jury.

Claims that arose before April 21, 2025 keep the older rule, under which the collateral source rule generally kept insurance payments away from the jury. The new rule mainly affects claims with large billed amounts and low insurance payments, and claims built on letter-of-protection care.

Other SB 68 changes that affect settlement value

  • Anchoring. Lawyers can argue a dollar figure for pain and suffering only in closing argument, and the figure must be rationally related to the evidence. A new number can’t be introduced for the first time in rebuttal (O.C.G.A. § 9-10-184).
  • Bifurcation. In injury and wrongful death cases, any party can ask to try fault first and damages second before the same jury. The request must be granted unless the amount in controversy is under $150,000 or a narrow exception applies (§ 51-12-15).
  • Voluntary dismissal. A plaintiff can dismiss without a court order only within 60 days after the defendant’s answer (§ 9-11-41).
  • Motions to dismiss. Discovery is stayed while a motion to dismiss is pending, and the defendant’s answer isn’t due until 15 days after it is decided (§ 9-11-12).
  • Negligent security. For claims arising on or after April 21, 2025, new statutes define when a property owner is liable for a crime committed by a third party on its property, require foreseeability based on prior similar incidents or a specific warning, and require the jury to apportion fault to the criminal (§§ 51-3-50 to 51-3-57).

Together these changes give insurers more room to argue for lower values at trial, which shows up in settlement offers. They don’t cap damages.

Damage caps in Georgia

Georgia has no cap on general damages in injury cases. The Georgia Supreme Court struck down the medical malpractice cap on non-economic damages in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery v. Nestlehutt (2010) as a violation of the right to a jury trial. The limits that remain are:

  • Punitive damages: require clear and convincing evidence of willful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness or conscious indifference, and are capped at $250,000 unless the defendant acted with specific intent to harm, was impaired by alcohol or drugs, or the claim is for product liability (§ 51-12-5.1).
  • The State of Georgia: $1,000,000 per person and $3,000,000 per occurrence under the Georgia Tort Claims Act, with no punitive damages (§ 50-21-29).

Malpractice claims for emergency room care have a higher standard of proof: the patient must prove gross negligence by clear and convincing evidence (§ 51-1-29.5). The malpractice calculator reflects that Georgia has no cap.

Wrongful death: the full value of the life

Georgia measures wrongful death damages differently from most states. The family recovers the “full value of the life of the decedent” from the decedent’s own perspective, without deducting personal living expenses (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2). That includes the economic value of the earnings the person would have had and the intangible value of living: relationships, experiences and the enjoyment of life. Grief of the survivors isn’t the measure; the value of the life is.

The claim belongs first to the surviving spouse, who shares it with the children, with the spouse receiving at least one third; if there is no spouse or child, to the parents; and otherwise to the estate’s administrator for the next of kin. A separate estate claim recovers medical and funeral expenses and the person’s own pain and suffering before death (§ 51-4-5). The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Demands, interest and offers of settlement

Georgia gives claimants three tools that put pressure on insurers:

  • Time-limited demands. A pre-suit offer to settle a motor vehicle, premises or bodily injury claim within policy limits must follow O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1, including a written offer, at least 30 days to accept, the amount, the type of release and the medical records. An insurer that unreasonably fails to accept a proper demand within limits can face a bad-faith claim for an excess verdict.
  • Unliquidated damages interest. If you send a written demand by certified mail under § 51-12-14 and the defendant doesn’t pay within 30 days, a later judgment at least as large as the demand earns interest at the prime rate plus 3% from the 30th day.
  • Offers of settlement. Under § 9-11-68, a defendant whose written offer is rejected can recover its attorney fees if the final judgment is less than 75% of the offer. A plaintiff whose offer is rejected can recover fees if the judgment is more than 125% of the offer.

The demand letter generator helps structure a demand. Have a lawyer check any time-limited demand against § 9-11-67.1 before it goes out, because a technical defect can defeat it.

Claims against government

The State of Georgia waives immunity for the negligence of state employees acting within their jobs, subject to the Georgia Tort Claims Act’s exceptions, its $1 million per person cap and its 12-month notice rule. Cities and counties have their own immunity rules. A common exception allows claims for the negligent use of a government motor vehicle, up to the amount of insurance or the statutory limits the government must carry. The six-month city deadline is the one most often missed. The notice must describe the time, place and extent of the injury and the amount claimed, so it should be prepared carefully and sent by a method that proves delivery.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls on business property. A business must keep the premises reasonably safe for customers (O.C.G.A. § 51-3-1). In a slip-and-fall case the question is usually whether the owner had superior knowledge of the hazard compared with the customer (Robinson v. Kroger Co., 1997). See the Georgia slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. An owner is liable if they knew the dog was vicious or dangerous and let it run at large, and a violation of a local leash law can establish that (§ 51-2-7). See the Georgia dog bite calculator.

Bars and hosts. A seller or host can be liable for serving alcohol to someone noticeably intoxicated, knowing that person will soon be driving, or for serving someone underage, when the intoxication causes injury (§ 51-1-40).

Liens and what you keep

  • Health insurers can be repaid from a settlement only if you have been fully compensated for all your losses, and their recovery is reduced by a share of attorney fees and costs (O.C.G.A. § 33-24-56.1). Federally governed self-funded plans and Medicare follow federal rules.
  • Hospitals and nursing homes can file liens on the cause of action for their charges (§ 44-14-470).
  • Settlements for children above $15,000 need court approval (§ 29-3-3).

The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves you.

How long Georgia claims take

Most Georgia crash claims settle without trial, often a few months after treatment ends and a demand package goes out. A time-limited demand starts a clock of at least 30 days for the insurer to respond. Lawsuits usually take one to three years, and SB 68’s stay of discovery during a motion to dismiss and the option to split trials into fault and damages phases can add time in contested cases. Metro Atlanta courts, particularly in Fulton, DeKalb and Gwinnett counties, handle a large share of the state’s injury trials. The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage, and the settlement offer checker compares an offer with your own estimate.

What to do in the first weeks

  • If a city vehicle or city property was involved, send the ante litem notice within six months. For a county or the state, within 12 months.
  • Find out whether your UM coverage is add-on or reduced-by, and report the claim to your own insurer.
  • Keep your health plan’s explanations of benefits. After SB 68, what was paid is part of the medical evidence.
  • If you were wearing a seat belt, make sure that is documented in the medical and police records.
  • Calendar the two-year deadline, and don’t count on criminal-case tolling without advice.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Two years from the injury in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Property damage claims have four years. Claims against a city need written notice within six months, and against a county or the state within 12 months.

faqs.question: Can I recover if I was partly at fault in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you were less than 50% responsible; your damages are reduced by your percentage. At 50% or more you recover nothing (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33).

faqs.question: Can a Georgia jury hear that I wasn’t wearing a seat belt?
faqs.answer: Yes. SB 68 changed O.C.G.A. § 40-8-76.1 in 2025 so that seat belt use is admissible on negligence, causation and apportionment of fault. Before that it was generally excluded.

faqs.question: What did Georgia’s 2025 tort reform change for injury claims?
faqs.answer: SB 68 allowed seat belt evidence, limited medical damages to the reasonable value of necessary care with evidence of amounts paid for claims arising after April 21, 2025, restricted dollar-figure arguments for pain and suffering, allowed split trials on fault and damages, and created negligent security rules.

faqs.question: Does Georgia cap pain and suffering?
faqs.answer: No. The Georgia Supreme Court struck down the malpractice cap in 2010, and there is no cap in other injury cases. Punitive damages are generally capped at $250,000, and claims against the state at $1 million per person.

faqs.question: What is add-on uninsured motorist coverage?
faqs.answer: Georgia’s default UM coverage, which pays on top of the at-fault driver’s liability limits rather than being reduced by them. Reduced-by coverage must be chosen in writing.
