north-carolina.metaTitle: North Carolina Personal Injury Laws 2026: Fault and Deadlines
north-carolina.metaDescription: How North Carolina’s contributory negligence rule, three-year deadline, 2025 insurance changes (50/100/50), Rule 414 and 50% lien cap affect a claim.
north-carolina.excerpt: North Carolina can bar your claim if you were even slightly at fault, so the exceptions matter. It gives you three years to sue and, since July 2025, higher insurance minimums and better UIM coverage. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
north-carolina.html:
How a North Carolina injury claim is valued

A North Carolina injury claim pays for medical expenses, lost earnings and other financial losses, plus pain and suffering, scarring, and permanent injury. There is no cap on those damages outside medical malpractice. On paper, the math looks like any other state’s.

The difference is fault. North Carolina is one of only a handful of jurisdictions that still use contributory negligence: if you were even slightly at fault for your own injury, you can be barred from recovering anything. That single rule shapes every North Carolina negotiation, and the exceptions to it, especially last clear chance and gross negligence, are where many claims are won or lost. This guide explains it, along with North Carolina’s three-year deadline, the insurance changes that took effect on July 1, 2025, and the state’s limits on medical bills and liens, with the statute or case behind each.

Run your own figures with the North Carolina car accident calculator or the North Carolina personal injury calculator.

A North Carolina claim, worked through

An example, not a forecast. A driver is hit by a car pulling out of a parking lot in Charlotte and treats for a neck injury, including injections. Providers billed $30,000; health insurance paid $17,500 and the providers accepted it. Lost wages are $7,000.

  • Medical expenses under North Carolina’s evidence rule: the $17,500 actually paid, not the $30,000 billed.
  • Economic damages: $17,500 plus $7,000 = $24,500.
  • Pain and suffering at two to three times the economic damages, and the claim before any fault issue: $73,500 to $98,000.

Now suppose the insurer finds a witness who says the injured driver was going a few miles over the limit. In most states that might cut the claim by 10%. In North Carolina, if a jury finds that the driver’s speed was a proximate cause of the crash, the recovery is zero. That is why North Carolina insurers deny claims over small fault arguments that adjusters elsewhere would simply discount, and why the evidence that you did nothing wrong deserves as much attention as the evidence of your injuries.

Contributory negligence

Under North Carolina common law, a plaintiff whose own negligence contributed to the injury, even slightly, can’t recover from a defendant whose negligence was ordinary rather than gross. The defense has to plead contributory negligence and prove it; the injured person doesn’t have to disprove it (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-139). Common contributory negligence arguments include speeding, following too closely, not keeping a proper lookout, walking outside a crosswalk, and for falls, failing to watch where you were going.

Exceptions that keep a claim alive

  • Last clear chance. If you were negligent and put yourself in a position of peril you couldn’t escape, and the defendant saw or should have seen your danger in time to avoid the harm but failed to use that chance, you can still recover. This doctrine comes up often in pedestrian cases.
  • Gross negligence or willful conduct. Ordinary contributory negligence isn’t a defense when the defendant’s conduct was grossly negligent or willful and wanton, such as racing or driving while heavily impaired. The plaintiff’s own gross negligence can still bar the claim.
  • Children. Very young children are presumed incapable of negligence, and older children are judged by what a child of the same age, experience and capacity would do.

North Carolina also keeps joint and several liability, the companion rule: when two or more defendants are at fault, each can be made to pay the whole judgment. That helps when one defendant has little insurance. The comparative fault calculator shows how North Carolina’s all-or-nothing rule compares with other states.

Seat belts

Not wearing a seat belt generally can’t be used as evidence of negligence, including contributory negligence, in a North Carolina civil case (§ 20-135.2A(d)). The insurer can’t use it to bar your claim.

Pedestrians and cyclists

Contributory negligence weighs heavily on people outside a car. A pedestrian crossing outside a marked or unmarked crosswalk must yield to vehicles (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-174), and the insurer will often argue that a pedestrian who didn’t yield was contributorily negligent. The same statute also requires every driver to use due care to avoid hitting a pedestrian, and the last clear chance doctrine was developed for cases like these: a driver who saw, or should have seen, a pedestrian in a helpless position and had time to stop can still be liable. Cyclists are treated as vehicle operators and must follow the rules of the road, including lighting requirements at night, so a missing headlight can become the defense. Photos of the scene, lighting conditions and the driver’s line of sight matter more here than in most states. The pedestrian accident calculator and the bicycle accident calculator apply North Carolina’s fault rule.

North Carolina filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: three years from the injury (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-52(16)).
  • Property damage: three years (§ 1-52).
  • Wrongful death: two years from the date of death (§ 1-53(4)).
  • Medical malpractice: three years from the last act of the provider, with up to one more year if the injury wasn’t discovered right away, and a four-year outer limit in most cases (§ 1-15(c)). The complaint must certify that a qualified expert reviewed the care and is willing to testify that it fell below the standard (Rule 9(j)).
  • Claims against the State: three years, filed with the North Carolina Industrial Commission under the State Tort Claims Act (§ 143-299).
  • Children: the deadline generally doesn’t run until the child turns 18 (§ 1-17), with special limits in malpractice cases.

Three years is longer than many states allow, but the two-year wrongful death period is shorter, and a claim that starts as an injury claim becomes a death claim with a different clock if the person dies. The North Carolina filing deadline calculator counts the dates.

Car insurance after July 1, 2025

North Carolina is an at-fault state. A 2023 law raised the minimum liability limits for policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2025 to $50,000 per person, $100,000 per crash and $50,000 for property damage, up from 30/60/25. Older policies keep their old limits until renewal, so for a crash in late 2025 or 2026 it matters when the at-fault driver’s policy last renewed.

The same law changed underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage in a way that helps injured people. Before, UIM was reduced by what the at-fault driver’s insurer paid. For policies issued or renewed since July 1, 2025, UIM is no longer offset by the liability payment, and whether a driver is “underinsured” is measured against your total damages rather than your own UIM limit. With $50,000 of liability coverage on the other side and $100,000 of your own UIM, a claim worth $200,000 can now recover up to $150,000 from the two coverages combined, instead of $100,000 under the old offset rule. New and renewed policies must include UM and UIM at least equal to the new minimums. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows how the coverages combine.

Medical payments coverage is optional and pays medical bills regardless of fault, which matters in a contributory negligence state: MedPay pays even if your own fault would bar a liability claim.

Medical bills: what was paid

Since 2011, North Carolina Rule of Evidence 414 limits evidence of past medical expenses to the amounts actually paid to satisfy the bills, plus the amounts actually necessary to satisfy bills that remain unpaid, regardless of who paid them (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 8C-1, Rule 414). Write-offs aren’t part of the claim. In the example above, that kept the medical figure at $17,500 rather than $30,000. For unpaid bills, the question becomes what amount would actually satisfy them, which can be disputed when care was given on a lien. Future medical costs are proven through testimony and aren’t limited by past discounts.

Damage limits in North Carolina

  • Ordinary injury cases: no cap on compensatory damages.
  • Medical malpractice: non-economic damages are capped at an amount adjusted every three years; the figure for 2026 is $712,847, per the state budget office (§ 90-21.19). The cap doesn’t apply when the injury involves permanent injury, disfigurement, loss of use of a body part or death and the provider’s conduct was reckless, grossly negligent, fraudulent or malicious.
  • Punitive damages: require fraud, malice or willful or wanton conduct proven by clear and convincing evidence, and are capped at three times compensatory damages or $250,000, whichever is greater (§ 1D-25). The cap doesn’t apply to injuries caused by a driver impaired by alcohol or drugs in certain circumstances (§ 1D-26).
  • The State: claims under the State Tort Claims Act are limited to $1,000,000 per person (§ 143-299.2).

The malpractice calculator applies the 2026 North Carolina cap.

Claims against government

Claims for negligence by State employees go to the Industrial Commission rather than to a jury, and the State can raise the claimant’s contributory negligence there too. Cities and counties have governmental immunity for governmental functions, such as police and road maintenance, but waive it to the extent they buy liability insurance (§§ 160A-485 and 153A-435). Whether a function is governmental or proprietary, and what the policy covers, often decides whether a claim against a local government can go forward. School buses and other specific programs have their own statutes. Get the government’s insurance information early.

Wrongful death claims

North Carolina’s wrongful death statute is broad on damages. The personal representative can recover medical and funeral expenses, the person’s own pain and suffering before death, the present value of the person’s net income, the services, protection, care and assistance they would have provided, and the family’s loss of society, companionship, comfort, guidance and advice, plus punitive damages in a proper case (§ 28A-18-2). The money is distributed under the intestate succession rules rather than the will.

The catch is contributory negligence: if the person who died was contributorily negligent, the death claim can be barred the same way an injury claim would be. The deadline is two years from the death. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. North Carolina owners owe all lawful visitors reasonable care to keep the premises safe, after Nelson v. Freeland (1998) did away with the old distinction between invitees and licensees. Contributory negligence is the usual defense: an owner will argue the hazard was obvious and the visitor should have seen it. See the North Carolina slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. Owners are strictly liable for injuries caused by a dog that has been declared dangerous (§ 67-4.4) and by dogs over six months old running at large at night (§ 67-12). Otherwise, the owner is liable if they knew or should have known of the dog’s dangerous tendencies. See the North Carolina dog bite calculator.

Bars. The Dram Shop Act allows claims against a permit holder that negligently sold alcohol to someone underage who then caused a crash while impaired, with damages capped at $500,000 (§§ 18B-121 and 18B-123). North Carolina courts also recognize a common-law negligence claim against a seller who served a visibly intoxicated person who it knew would be driving.

Hurt at work in North Carolina

Workers’ compensation is the exclusive remedy against an employer for most workplace injuries, and it pays regardless of fault, which removes contributory negligence from the comp claim. A lawsuit against the employer is allowed only in narrow cases where the employer intentionally engaged in misconduct knowing it was substantially certain to cause serious injury or death (Woodson v. Rowland, 1991). A claim against a third party, such as a negligent driver, a property owner or an equipment maker, can proceed alongside the comp claim, and contributory negligence does apply there. When the third-party claim recovers money, the employer or its insurer has a lien for the benefits it paid, and a superior court judge can reduce that lien in some circumstances (§ 97-10.2). The construction accident calculator takes the comp lien into account.

Medical liens: the 50% limit

North Carolina caps how much of a settlement medical providers can take. Under §§ 44-49 and 44-50, liens of doctors, hospitals and other providers attach to the recovery, but all of them together can’t exceed 50% of the amount recovered after attorney fees. For example, on a $60,000 settlement with a one-third fee of $20,000, the providers’ combined liens can’t exceed $20,000, even if they claim $22,000. Providers usually share that amount in proportion to their bills. The limit doesn’t control Medicare, Medicaid, workers’ compensation or self-funded employer health plans governed by federal law, which have their own repayment rules.

The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves you. Settlements for children need court approval.

Interest, offers and timing

When an injury case goes to judgment, North Carolina adds interest at the legal rate of 8% a year on the compensatory damages from the date the lawsuit was filed (§§ 24-1 and 24-5(b)). A defendant can make a formal offer of judgment under Rule 68; if the plaintiff rejects it and then does no better at trial, the plaintiff bears the costs incurred after the offer. Claims up to $10,000 can be filed in small claims court before a magistrate. Most crash claims settle with the insurer months after treatment ends, and the contributory negligence defense is the main reason some don’t. The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage.

Trucks, rideshare and other commercial vehicles

Interstate trucking companies must carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage under federal rules, and a claim against the company can rest on its own failures in hiring, training, maintenance and hours-of-service compliance as well as on the driver’s conduct. Rideshare companies carry much higher limits once a ride has been accepted than while a driver is only logged into the app. In these cases, a defendant’s gross negligence, such as a driver far beyond hours-of-service limits, can also take contributory negligence off the table. The North Carolina truck accident calculator uses the federal limits.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Collect the evidence that you weren’t at fault: photos, video, witnesses, the police report and, after a crash, the vehicle data. In North Carolina this evidence is the claim.
  • Don’t give the other driver’s insurer a recorded statement without advice. Small admissions about speed or attention are how contributory negligence defenses start.
  • Check when the at-fault driver’s policy last renewed, and your own UIM limits. The July 2025 changes depend on renewal dates.
  • Use MedPay if you have it. It pays regardless of fault.
  • Keep the explanations of benefits for every bill. Rule 414 makes the amounts paid the medical number that matters.
  • If the other side claims you were partly at fault, write down exactly what happened while you still remember it, including where you were looking, your speed and the lighting. Last clear chance and gross negligence arguments depend on those details.
  • Calendar the three-year deadline, and the two-year deadline if the injured person has died.

faqs.answer: Only in medical malpractice, where the non-economic cap is $712,847 for 2026, with exceptions for reckless or malicious conduct causing serious harm. Other injury claims have no cap.

michigan.metaTitle: Michigan Personal Injury Laws 2026: No-Fault and Threshold
michigan.metaDescription: How Michigan no-fault PIP choices, the serious impairment threshold, the 51% rule, three-year deadline, $3,000 mini-tort and 2026 malpractice caps work.
michigan.excerpt: Michigan’s no-fault system pays your medical bills and most lost wages regardless of fault, but pain and suffering requires a serious impairment, and since 2020 drivers choose their PIP and liability limits. Here is how each rule works, with the statute behind it.
michigan.html:
How a Michigan injury claim is valued

Michigan splits most car crash claims in two. Your own no-fault insurer pays your medical expenses, a large share of lost wages and household help, whoever caused the crash. Then, separately, you can sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering if the injury meets Michigan’s threshold, and for economic losses no-fault doesn’t cover. Claims that don’t involve a car, such as falls, dog bites and malpractice, follow ordinary negligence rules with Michigan’s own twists.

The 2019 no-fault reform, which took effect for policies issued or renewed after July 1, 2020, changed both halves of the system: it let drivers choose lower PIP medical limits, set a fee schedule for providers, raised the default liability limits and wrote the serious-impairment threshold into the statute. This guide explains how those rules work today, along with Michigan’s fault rule, deadlines and damage caps, with the statute or case behind each. Run your own figures with the Michigan car accident calculator, which applies no-fault and the threshold, or the Michigan personal injury calculator.

A Michigan crash claim, worked through

An example, not a prediction. A driver is rear-ended on US-131 in Grand Rapids and tears a knee ligament that needs surgery and eight months off work. Medical costs of $60,000 are paid by the driver’s own PIP coverage, chosen at the $250,000 level. The driver earns $7,000 a month, so the lost income is $56,000; PIP pays 85% of it, leaving about $8,400 unpaid. The at-fault driver’s insurer argues the injured driver braked abruptly and was 25% at fault.

  • From PIP, regardless of fault: the $60,000 medical and 85% of wages, up to the monthly cap.
  • From the at-fault driver, economic losses PIP didn’t pay: about $8,400 of wage loss.
  • Surgery and months of restricted activity meet the serious-impairment threshold, so non-economic damages are available. At two to three times the total economic loss of $116,000: $232,000 to $348,000.
  • Tort claim after a 25% fault reduction: $180,300 to $267,300.

Whether that tort claim is collectible depends on the at-fault driver’s bodily injury limit. Policies default to $250,000 per person, but a driver can choose $50,000, and in that case your own underinsured motorist coverage, if you bought it, has to fill the gap. If the injured driver had been more than 50% at fault, the non-economic damages would be barred, though PIP benefits would still be paid.

PIP: what your own policy pays

Personal protection insurance (PIP) pays benefits regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107):

  • Allowable expenses: reasonable and necessary medical care, rehabilitation, attendant care and other care costs, up to the medical limit you chose.
  • Work loss: 85% of gross income for up to three years after the crash, up to a monthly maximum that is adjusted every year.
  • Replacement services: up to $20 a day for household help such as chores and driving, for up to three years.
  • Survivor’s loss benefits for dependents if the injured person dies.

The PIP medical limit you chose

Since July 2, 2020, drivers choose a PIP medical limit (MCL 500.3107c): unlimited, $500,000, $250,000, $250,000 with some household members excluded because they have qualifying health coverage, $50,000 for Medicaid enrollees, or no PIP medical coverage for people with Medicare Parts A and B. Policies issued before the reform were unlimited. When PIP medical runs out, your health insurance and the at-fault driver become the sources for the rest. Choosing a low limit doesn’t change your right to sue the at-fault driver for medical costs above it.

The fee schedule and attendant care

The reform limited what providers can charge PIP insurers to percentages of Medicare rates (MCL 500.3157) and capped family-provided attendant care at 56 hours a week. In Andary v. USAA (2023), the Michigan Supreme Court held that those limits don’t apply to people injured before the reform took effect on June 11, 2019, who keep the benefits their policies promised. The no-fault and PIP calculator estimates what PIP pays.

Pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists

PIP follows a priority order that decides which insurer pays (MCL 500.3114 and 500.3115). A pedestrian or cyclist hit by a car usually claims PIP first from a policy in their own household, as the named insured, a spouse or a resident relative. If no household policy exists, the insurer of the vehicle involved pays, and if there is none, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan assigns an insurer. Choosing a low PIP limit on your own car policy can therefore matter even when you are walking.

Motorcyclists are treated differently. A motorcycle isn’t a “motor vehicle” for no-fault purposes, so a rider gets PIP only when a car or truck is involved in the crash, and the insurer of that vehicle’s owner or driver is generally first in line to pay, ahead of the rider’s own auto policy. A rider hurt in a crash with no other vehicle involved gets no PIP and relies on health insurance and any medical payments coverage on the motorcycle policy. The motorcycle accident calculator and the pedestrian accident calculator apply these rules.

PIP deadlines: the one-year rules

PIP has its own deadlines, separate from the lawsuit deadline against the driver (MCL 500.3145):

  • You must give written notice of injury to the insurer, or have received a payment from it, within one year after the crash.
  • A lawsuit for unpaid PIP benefits can recover only losses incurred within one year before the suit was filed, the “one-year-back” rule. Since the reform, that period is paused from the time a specific claim is made until the insurer formally denies it.

If you don’t know which insurer is responsible, for example when no household policy exists, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan assigns one; the same one-year notice rule applies.

The serious-impairment threshold

You can sue the at-fault driver for non-economic damages, such as pain, suffering and lost enjoyment of life, only if the injury caused death, permanent serious disfigurement, or serious impairment of a body function (MCL 500.3135(1)). The 2019 reform wrote into the statute the test from McCormick v. Carrier (2010): a serious impairment is an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects the person’s general ability to lead their normal life (MCL 500.3135(5)). It doesn’t have to be permanent, and it doesn’t have to affect every part of the person’s life; the question is whether it affected the ability to lead their own pre-crash life, for however long it lasted.

Objective manifestation means the impairment can be observed or perceived by someone other than the injured person, often through imaging, surgery, measured loss of motion or a doctor’s documented restrictions. Pain alone, without a medically identifiable cause, usually isn’t enough.

Other claims against the at-fault driver

  • Excess economic loss. Medical costs above your PIP limit, wage loss beyond three years or above the monthly cap, and the 15% of wages PIP doesn’t pay can be claimed from the at-fault driver without meeting the threshold (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)).
  • Mini-tort. Up to $3,000 for damage to your vehicle that your own insurance didn’t cover, such as your collision deductible (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)). Like other tort damages, it is reduced by your share of fault and isn’t available if you were more than 50% at fault or were driving without the required insurance.

Fault: the 51% rule for non-economic damages

Michigan reduces damages by the injured person’s percentage of fault. If you are more than 50% at fault, you can’t recover non-economic damages at all, though you can still recover economic damages reduced by your share (MCL 600.2959 and 500.3135(2)). PIP benefits aren’t affected by fault.

Not wearing a seat belt can be considered evidence of negligence in a car crash case, but it can’t reduce your recovery by more than 5% (MCL 257.710e). Michigan generally doesn’t make one defendant pay another’s share; each pays its own percentage, with exceptions such as some medical malpractice cases (MCL 600.2956). Michigan filing deadlines

  • Personal injury: three years from the injury (MCL 600.5805).
  • Wrongful death: the underlying claim’s period, generally three years, with a saving provision that lets the personal representative file within two years after appointment, if no more than three years after the original period ended (MCL 600.5852).
  • Medical malpractice: two years from the act, or six months from when the injury was or should have been discovered, with a six-year outer limit in most cases (MCL 600.5805 and 600.5838a). You must send a notice of intent and wait 182 days before filing (MCL 600.2912b), and file an affidavit of merit from a qualified expert with the complaint (MCL 600.2912d).
  • PIP benefits: notice within one year, and the one-year-back rule (above).
  • Road defects: written notice to the government agency within 120 days of the injury (MCL 691.1404).
  • Claims against the State: in the Court of Claims, with a notice of intention or the claim itself filed within six months for personal injury (MCL 600.6431).

The Michigan filing deadline calculator counts these dates.

Liability limits and UM/UIM coverage

Since the reform, bodily injury liability coverage defaults to $250,000 per person and $500,000 per crash. A driver can choose lower limits, down to $50,000 and $100,000, by signing a form (MCL 500.3009). Michigan no-fault also includes $1,000,000 of property protection insurance for damage your car does to other people’s property in Michigan, and $10,000 of property damage liability for crashes in other states.

Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage is optional in Michigan. Because a driver can now pick $50,000 limits, UIM on your own policy is often what pays a serious claim. Check your declarations page. The policy limits and UM/UIM calculator shows how much the coverages can pay.

Trucks and commercial vehicles

A crash with a commercial truck often has more insurance behind it than any personal policy. Interstate freight carriers must carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage under federal rules, and the company can be liable for its own negligence in hiring, training, maintenance and hours-of-service compliance. In Michigan the injured person’s PIP benefits still come through the normal priority order, but the tort claim for pain and suffering and excess economic loss runs against the driver and the carrier. Send the carrier a written request to preserve its driver logs, electronic data and dashcam video early. The Michigan truck accident calculator uses the federal limits.

How Michigan claims move

A Michigan crash often produces two claims on different tracks: a first-party claim against your own PIP insurer for benefits, and a third-party claim against the at-fault driver. PIP disputes, such as denied bills or cut-off wage benefits, are often litigated separately and sometimes by providers directly. The tort claim usually waits until treatment has progressed far enough to show whether the threshold is met. Many circuit courts send civil cases to case evaluation, where a panel of three lawyers places a value on the case that either side can accept or reject. The settlement timeline calculator estimates each stage, and the settlement offer checker compares an offer with your estimate.

Medical malpractice caps

Michigan caps non-economic damages in malpractice cases at amounts adjusted each year by the state Treasurer (MCL 600.1483). For 2026 the lower cap is $596,400. A higher cap of $1,065,000 applies when the patient was left paralyzed by a brain or spinal cord injury, with cognitive impairment so severe that they can’t make independent life decisions or care for themselves, or with permanent damage to a reproductive organ that prevents having children. Economic damages aren’t capped. The malpractice calculator applies the 2026 Michigan caps.

Claims against government

The Governmental Tort Liability Act gives government agencies broad immunity, with exceptions for defects in highways the agency is responsible for, negligent operation of government vehicles by employees, dangerous or defective public buildings, and proprietary functions (MCL 691.1402 to 691.1413). Individual employees are liable only for gross negligence that was the proximate cause of the injury (MCL 691.1407). The highway exception has the shortest fuse: a written notice describing the defect, the injury and the witnesses must reach the agency within 120 days. Potholes and broken sidewalks are common examples, and the agency often argues it had no notice of the defect.

Wrongful death

Michigan’s wrongful death act lets the personal representative recover medical, funeral and burial expenses, the person’s conscious pain and suffering before death, lost financial support and services, and the family’s loss of society and companionship (MCL 600.2922). The court divides the recovery among the family. In a car crash case, no-fault survivor’s loss benefits pay dependents separately, and the tort claim is subject to the same threshold rules, which are met by the death itself. The wrongful death calculator estimates the family’s claim.

Falls, dog bites and bars

Falls. For years Michigan owners could avoid liability by showing a hazard was “open and obvious.” In Kandil-Elsayed v. F & E Oil (2023), the Michigan Supreme Court changed that: whether a danger was open and obvious is now considered when deciding whether the owner breached its duty and how fault is shared, rather than wiping out the duty altogether. That has made more fall claims viable, with the injured person’s own carelessness reducing the award. See the Michigan slip and fall calculator.

Dog bites. Owners are strictly liable when their dog bites someone, without provocation, who is lawfully on public or private property (MCL 287.351), whether or not the dog had bitten before. See the Michigan dog bite calculator.

Bars. The dram shop act allows claims against a licensee that sold alcohol to a visibly intoxicated person or a minor, when that sale caused the injury (MCL 436.1801). You must give the bar written notice within 120 days after hiring a lawyer for the claim, and you must keep the intoxicated person in the lawsuit until it ends.

Interest, liens and what you keep

Michigan judgments earn interest from the date the complaint was filed (MCL 600.6013), which gives insurers a reason to settle cases that are likely to win. From the settlement itself come the lawyer’s contingency fee, typically one third for the tort claim, case costs, and any reimbursement claims from Medicare, Medicaid or a health plan for costs they paid that no-fault didn’t. If you chose coordinated coverage, your health insurer pays medical bills first and PIP is secondary, which affects who has a claim on the settlement. The medical lien calculator and the attorney fee calculator show what a settlement leaves you. Settlements for children need court approval.

What to do in the first weeks

  • Send your auto insurer a written application for PIP benefits right away, and keep proof of when you sent it.
  • Find your declarations page and note your PIP medical limit, whether coverage is coordinated, and your UIM limits.
  • If a road defect caused the crash or fall, send the 120-day notice to the right agency.
  • Ask your doctors to document restrictions on work, driving, sleep and daily activities. That record is the threshold evidence.
  • Submit wage records to the PIP insurer, and track the 15% of income PIP doesn’t replace.

faqs.question: Can I sue for pain and suffering after a Michigan car accident?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the crash caused death, permanent serious disfigurement or a serious impairment of a body function: an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects your general ability to lead your normal life (MCL 500.3135). It doesn’t have to be permanent.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file an injury lawsuit in Michigan?
faqs.answer: Three years from the injury for a claim against the at-fault party (MCL 600.5805). PIP claims need written notice within one year, and road defect claims need notice to the agency within 120 days.

faqs.question: What does Michigan PIP pay?
faqs.answer: Medical and care expenses up to the limit you chose, 85% of lost gross income for up to three years up to a monthly cap, up to $20 a day for replacement services, and survivor’s benefits.

faqs.question: What is the Michigan mini-tort?
faqs.answer: A claim for up to $3,000 against an at-fault driver for vehicle damage your insurance didn’t cover, such as your collision deductible (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)). It is reduced by your share of fault and isn’t available if you were more than 50% at fault.

faqs.question: Can I recover if I was partly at fault in Michigan?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your damages are reduced by your share. If you are more than 50% at fault you lose non-economic damages but can still recover reduced economic damages, and your PIP benefits are paid regardless.

faqs.question: What are Michigan’s medical malpractice caps for 2026?
faqs.answer: $596,400 for non-economic damages in most cases and $1,065,000 for certain catastrophic injuries, such as paralysis from a brain or spinal cord injury or severe permanent cognitive impairment (MCL 600.1483).
